questionText: What is the difference between a DTO and an entity in Spring Boot JSON handling?

target.learningOutcome: The learner can distinguish an API DTO from a persistence entity, explain the security and compatibility boundary, and map a deliberately limited response shape.
inScope: Persistent entity identity, state, relationships, and lifecycle
outOfScope: A full Jakarta Persistence mapping tutorial

claims.statement: A Jakarta Persistence entity has persistent identity and state and participates in a lifecycle managed through a persistence context, including mapped relationships where declared.
A request or response DTO models the fields owned by one public API operation rather than automatically publishing every field and relationship in the persistence model.
Separating DTOs from entities prevents ordinary JSON binding from accepting absent server-owned fields and prevents response mapping from exposing fields omitted by the response type.

Jakarta Persistence allows relationships to use lazy fetching, whose data need not be available after detachment, so an API should not make serializer traversal of an entity graph its public response contract.

examples.title: Compile and test the exact entity-to-response DTO mapper

validation.command: Run mvn -q test with Java 17 and the Spring Boot 3.3.1 managed Jackson version against the exact UserMappingExample
validation.expected: The serialized UserResponse contains id and displayName and has no email, passwordHash, or persistence version field

visuals.title: Request DTO, entity, and response DTO compared by purpose, fields, and boundary

notes: The lesson does not claim that DTOs are free; it explicitly names extra classes and mapping code as the trade-off.
The code demonstrates the security boundary by construction rather than relying on serializer annotations to hide internal fields.

review.notes: Entity identity, lifecycle, version, relationship, and lazy-fetch boundaries were checked against Jakarta Persistence 3.1; Spring JSON-binding behavior was checked against official Spring documentation. The Java 17 mapping test passed and proved sensitive-field absence.
